q: The United States and China should negotiate a binding treaty limiting the largest AI training runs, even if verification is imperfect.
r: The United States and China should not negotiate a binding treaty limiting AI training runs while verification remains imperfect.
p: Washington and Beijing should sign a training-run treaty now, imperfect verification and all.

q: Democracies should race to build superintelligence before authoritarian states, because who gets there first matters more than how carefully.
r: Democracies should not race to build superintelligence; how carefully it is built matters more than who gets there first.
p: The free world must win the superintelligence race; caution is secondary.

q: An international AI agency modeled on the nuclear watchdog should be created with inspection rights over frontier labs in all member states.
r: No international AI agency with inspection rights over frontier labs should be created.
p: Build an AI version of the nuclear watchdog, with the right to inspect labs.

q: Interoperable national standards are a better goal for international AI governance than harmonized laws.
r: Harmonized laws are a better goal for international AI governance than interoperable national standards.
p: Aim for standards that talk to each other, not identical laws everywhere.

q: The UN scientific panel on AI should be given authority to issue binding capability assessments that trigger obligations under national law.
r: The UN scientific panel on AI should remain advisory, with no authority to trigger obligations under national law.
p: The UN's AI science panel should have teeth: its findings should trigger legal duties.

q: International AI summits and declarations have produced no meaningful constraint on any lab and should be discontinued.
r: International AI summits and declarations have produced meaningful constraints and should continue.
p: The summit circuit has changed nothing; stop holding them.

q: Allied governments should share frontier model evaluations with China to reduce accident risk, even though this reveals capability information.
r: Allied governments should not share frontier model evaluations with China, because it reveals capability information.
p: Sharing eval results with China is worth the capability leakage if it prevents accidents.

q: Countries without frontier labs should have no vote on rules governing frontier AI development.
r: Countries without frontier labs should have a vote on rules governing frontier AI development.
p: If you do not build frontier AI, you should not vote on its rules.

q: The international legally binding AI convention should be ratified by every democracy, even though it constrains domestic flexibility.
r: Democracies should not ratify the international legally binding AI convention because it constrains domestic flexibility.
p: Every democracy should sign up to the binding AI convention despite the loss of flexibility.

q: Competition between the US and China will produce safer AI than cooperation would, because each side must demonstrate reliability.
r: Cooperation between the US and China would produce safer AI than competition, because racing erodes safety margins.
p: Rivalry, not cooperation, is what will make AI safe.

q: Frontier labs should be prohibited from opening research offices in countries that refuse to join international safety agreements.
r: Frontier labs should be free to open research offices in any country regardless of its participation in safety agreements.
p: Labs should not set up shop in countries that stay out of AI safety agreements.

q: Every country should develop sovereign frontier AI capability rather than depend on models from the US or China.
r: Most countries should rely on models from the US or China rather than pursue sovereign frontier AI capability.
p: Each nation should build its own frontier AI instead of importing it.

q: AI-enabled cyber operations against another state's civilian infrastructure should be banned by treaty, with mandatory attribution mechanisms.
r: AI-enabled cyber operations should not be singled out for a treaty ban distinct from existing cyber norms.
p: A treaty should ban AI cyberattacks on civilian infrastructure and require attribution.

q: A single global AI regulator would be worse than no international coordination at all.
r: A single global AI regulator would be better than no international coordination at all.
p: One world AI regulator would be a bigger mistake than having none.

q: Wealthy countries should fund compute access for lower-income countries as a condition of any international AI agreement.
r: Compute access funding for lower-income countries should not be a condition of international AI agreements.
p: Any AI agreement should include rich countries paying for poorer countries' compute.

q: China's AI governance, with its binding rules on generative AI and deepfakes, is more effective than the US approach.
r: The US approach to AI governance is more effective than China's binding rules on generative AI and deepfakes.
p: China's binding AI rules work better than America's patchwork.

q: Frontier labs in allied countries should pool their most dangerous capability evaluations under one international body rather than each running its own.
r: Frontier labs should each run their own dangerous capability evaluations rather than pooling them under an international body.
p: The scariest evals should be run once, jointly, by an international body.

q: Middle powers like the UAE and Saudi Arabia should be free to host frontier compute for any developer, regardless of US or Chinese objections.
r: Middle powers should not host frontier compute for developers when the US or China objects.
p: Gulf states and others should host frontier compute for whomever they like.

q: Nations should agree to a mutual ban on using AI to interfere in each other's elections, with verification by an independent body.
r: An international ban on AI election interference is unenforceable and should not be pursued.
p: Countries should sign a verified pledge not to use AI against each other's elections.

q: Energy infrastructure, not chip access, will decide which country leads in AI over the next decade.
r: Chip access, not energy infrastructure, will decide which country leads in AI over the next decade.
x: energy versus chips as decisive input
p: The AI race will be won on power plants, not on chips.

q: Any country developing frontier AI should be required to host an international AI safety institute office with access to its labs.
r: Countries developing frontier AI should not be required to host international safety institute offices.
p: Frontier countries should have to host an international safety office with lab access.

q: The EU's AI regulation has made Europe irrelevant to frontier AI and should be substantially repealed.
r: The EU's AI regulation has not made Europe irrelevant to frontier AI and should not be substantially repealed.
p: Europe regulated itself out of the AI frontier and should undo it.

q: A global moratorium on training runs above the current frontier should be adopted until international verification tools exist.
r: No global moratorium on training runs should be adopted while verification tools are developed.
p: The world should freeze frontier training until it can verify compliance.

q: Export controls are a form of economic warfare that will make AI conflict more likely, not less.
r: Export controls reduce the likelihood of AI conflict rather than increase it.
p: Chip controls are economic warfare and raise the odds of real conflict.

q: Frontier labs should be required to give the same pre-release access to allied governments that they give to their home government.
r: Frontier labs should not be required to give allied governments the same pre-release access as their home government.
p: Allies should get the same early look at frontier models as the home government.

q: Regional AI frameworks in Africa, ASEAN, and Latin America matter more for most of humanity than anything decided in Washington or Brussels.
r: Decisions in Washington and Brussels matter more for most of humanity than regional AI frameworks in Africa, ASEAN, and Latin America.
x: where governance matters for most people
p: For most of the world, regional AI rules will count for more than US or EU decisions.

q: Nations should agree that no AI system may be given authority to launch nuclear weapons, and verify this through mutual inspection.
r: An agreement excluding AI from nuclear launch authority is unnecessary because no nation would delegate that authority anyway.
p: A verified treaty should keep AI out of nuclear launch decisions.

q: Multinational companies, not governments, will and should set the effective global rules for AI.
r: Governments, not multinational companies, will and should set the effective global rules for AI.
p: The real global AI rules will come from companies, and that is fine.

q: Countries should agree to jointly fund and govern a shared international frontier AI project, as they did for particle physics.
r: Countries should not attempt a jointly funded international frontier AI project.
p: Frontier AI should have its own international laboratory, jointly funded like particle physics.

q: It would be better for the world if China reached frontier AI parity with the US than if the US kept a large lead.
r: It would be better for the world if the US kept a large frontier AI lead than if China reached parity.
p: A world with US-China AI parity beats one with a lopsided American lead.
